summary: Describes an authentication option for the Telnet protocol: a generic method to negotiate an authentication type and mode, including whether to encrypt and whether to forward credentials.

eli5.summary: Telnet originally just trusted who you said you were. This adds a way for both sides to agree on how to prove identity.

questions: how do you encrypt a telnet session
subtitle: How a Telnet client and server agree on a way to prove identity, switch on encryption and pass credentials along.

tldr.problem: To log in over Telnet, users type passwords that cross the network in clear text, so anyone watching packets on an untrusted network can steal them.
tldr.mechanism: The AUTHENTICATION option (option 37) lets the server offer an ordered list of authentication type pairs. The client answers with authentication data, and a modifier byte says who authenticates whom, whether encryption is used and whether credentials are forwarded.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework only: each authentication type is defined in a separate document. RFC 2941 obsoletes RFC 1416 so the option can securely enable the Telnet encryption option.

today: RFC 2941 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2000. It obsoletes RFC 1416, and the metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Telnet Needs Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC names a deficiency in Telnet: to log in to a remote system, users type passwords that are passed in clear text through the network. If the connection crosses untrusted networks, someone watching packets in transit may compromise the passwords.

The AUTHENTICATION option is a framework for passing authentication information through the Telnet session, plus a way to enable encryption of the data stream, either as a side effect of successful authentication or through the separate Telnet ENCRYPT option. The RFC lists three benefits: the password is not sent in clear text, a front-end Telnet process that already holds credentials can send them automatically so the user types no password, and once authentication succeeds the stream can be encrypted against active attacks.

It is meant to be general enough to carry information for any authentication and encryption system. The document does not define a specific authentication type; separate documents are to be published for each one.
sections.eli5: Typing a password into old Telnet is like writing it on a postcard. This option lets the computers use a sealed envelope instead.

sections.title: Commands and Who Sends Them
sections.content:
Here the server is the side that did the passive TCP open (the LISTEN state) and the client is the side that did the active open. The option has the code AUTHENTICATION = 37.

Negotiation runs in one direction only. The server sends IAC DO AUTHENTICATION and the client answers IAC WILL AUTHENTICATION. A server that receives a DO must reply WONT, and a client that receives a WILL must reply DONT. The RFC explains why: there are three cases (server authenticates client, client authenticates server, or both), and negotiating in one direction and picking the case in the suboption removes ambiguity.

After that the server may request credentials at any time while the client is WILL, and four suboption commands are used, with strict roles:

  • SEND (code 1): only the server sends it, with an ordered list of authentication type pairs, most preferred first.
  • IS (code 0): only the client sends it, with its authentication data.
  • REPLY (code 2): only the server sends it, answering an IS. As many IS and REPLY messages may be exchanged as the chosen scheme needs.
  • NAME (code 3): an optional message from the client naming the account it wants to use. Authentication can succeed even if authorization for that account fails.

If the client supports none of the offered types it answers with type NULL, and the server may close the connection. When the server decides authentication cannot be negotiated, it should send IAC DONT AUTH. The default is WONT AUTHENTICATION DONT AUTHENTICATION, meaning no authentication information is exchanged.
sections.eli5: The server asks, in order of favorite first, which secret handshakes the client knows. The client picks one and they do it together.

sections.title: Type Pairs and Modifier Bits
sections.content:
An authentication-type-pair is two octets: the authentication type, and a modifier. The registered types run from NULL (0), KERBEROS_V4 (1) and KERBEROS_V5 (2) up to NTLM (15), and the RFC marks several of them with an asterisk to say they were never submitted to the IETF as an Internet standard. Future numbers are assigned by IANA on a First Come First Served basis.

The modifier carries several one-bit fields:

  • Who and how. AUTH_WHO_MASK and AUTH_HOW_MASK are read as a pair. The four combinations are client to server one way (the server authenticates the user), server to client one way (the server proves itself), and the two mutual variants in either order.
  • Encryption. ENCRYPT_OFF means no encryption and TELOPT ENCRYPT SHOULD NOT be negotiated. It MUST be used with types that provide no shared secret for a session key. ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT means TELOPT ENCRYPT MUST be negotiated in both directions right after authentication, before credentials forwarding, other options or user data, and a failure MUST end the session. ENCRYPT_AFTER_EXCHANGE turns encryption on in both directions right after the shared secret is exchanged, and the algorithm MUST be implied by the type.
  • Credential forwarding. INI_CRED_FWD_ON advises the server that the client will forward credentials right after authentication, and encryption if any, completes. Setting it when the mechanism cannot forward credentials is a protocol error. Forwarding MUST NOT be done after one-way client-to-server authentication, because the server's identity is not assured, and SHOULD NOT be done on an unprotected connection.

Older implementations do not understand the encryption and forwarding bits, so a sender that needs backward compatibility should offer pairs with these bits both set and not set.
sections.eli5: Each handshake offer comes with a few tick boxes: who proves who they are, whether to scramble the chat afterwards, and whether to pass along a permission slip.

sections.title: Worked Exchanges
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three examples. In the first, the server sends DO AUTHENTICATION and the client answers WILL AUTHENTICATION. The server then offers Kerberos 4 with mutual authentication and, as a fallback, Kerberos 4 with one-way authentication. The client sends its NAME ("joe") and an IS message with the Kerberos ticket. The server replies ACCEPT, the client sends a CHALLENGE, and the server proves who it is with a RESPONSE.

The second example is the same flow with ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT added, ending with both sides negotiating the Telnet ENCRYPT option in each direction. If that fails in either direction, the connection must be terminated immediately.

The third uses KEA_SJ with ENCRYPT_AFTER_EXCHANGE, where encryption starts inside the authentication exchange itself: the client starts encrypting after its third message and the server after its fourth. The RFC also says any implementation that supports the option is expected to support all of the specification.
sections.eli5: The examples show the whole conversation: hello, here is who I am, here is my proof, now prove who you are, and finally switching to secret code.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The weak point is the negotiation itself. When types are negotiated nothing has been authenticated yet, so neither side knows who it is talking to, and an intruder could try to steer the pair toward a weak or already compromised type. The type pair is not protected, so an attacker can force the weakest method both sides accept. An implementation should accept a type only if it is willing to trust it. The username sent in NAME is also unprotected and should be verified by a secure method before use.

If encryption must be turned on by a separate ENCRYPT negotiation, there is a window of vulnerability after authentication finishes. A server avoids it by offering only pairs with ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT set. Types that tie encryption to authentication also protect against an active attacker. A client SHOULD NOT support turning encryption off, and if re-enabling it fails it MUST terminate the connection.

The type pair must be integrity protected at the end of the exchange, which each type has to specify. Each side MUST check that the pair is consistent in every message, and any variation is a fatal protocol error.
sections.eli5: The risk is a sneaky person tricking both sides into using the weakest lock before either has proved who they are. So both sides must double-check, and only agree to locks they truly trust.

sections.title: User Interface Guidance
sections.content:
Although protocol documents rarely cover user interfaces, this one gives minimum guidance. The user MUST be able to say whether authentication is used and whether encryption is used when authentication succeeds. There SHOULD be at least four settings: REQUIRE (on failure show an error and end the connection), PROMPT (on failure show an error and ask before continuing), WARN (on failure show an error and continue) and DISABLE (do not try authentication).

The encryption switch SHOULD have the same settings, though it only applies after successful authentication. The default for both switches should be WARN, and the two may be implemented as a single switch.
sections.eli5: You get a dial: insist on the lock, ask me first, just warn me, or skip it.

items.label: AUTH_CLIENT_TO_SERVER
items.desc: The client authenticates to the server (AUTH_WHO_MASK is 1).

items.label: AUTH_SERVER_TO_CLIENT
items.desc: The server authenticates to the client.

items.label: ENCRYPT_AFTER_EXCHANGE
items.desc: Encryption starts after the shared secret is exchanged.
